The way the post-direction strategy works is that instead of jumping in to help at the first sign of trouble, you will allow them to struggle.

q: Here's the thing: to build argumentative ballers over the course of the year, I'm experimenting with a new idea this year: start slow. And so I've actually started debates this year without actually debating.

Quite simply, the kids weren't arguing at all. They were arranged on different teams, they alternated turns in speaking, but they literally could receive credit for not listening to a word anyone else said. And that was intentional.
I would argue the most critical part of an argument isn't the speaking part; it's the listening, understanding, and figuring out what to do with someone else's viewpoint.

I will be open and honest to admit that, too often, my students have not gotten here; they have focused too much on the game-like elements of debate and, ironically, this has made them mediocre at the game. You see, you can't really argue with anyone until you've fully understood and weighed their argument.

Why? Because I'll be giving students credit based on their ability to paraphrase and respond to another argument. Today I taught them the concept of flowing — of taking notes on the debates — but there was little incentive to do it.

But pound for pound, minute for minute, debates deliver more teachable moments, more writing connections, more motivation, more wow-factor, more student mindset shifts, and more results than just about anything else that I do in my classroom.
Don't read me wrong: they can't be all that we do. But they should be a regular occasion. I'd aim for once a month at least.

t: Why You Shouldn't Pep-Talk Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/09/21/why-you-shouldnt-pep-talk-difficult-students/
q: The student stands wordlessly, eyes averted, still smarting from yet another backslide as the earnest teacher softens the blows of the student’s many transgressions.
But pulling difficult students aside for pep-talks, particularly in response to recent misbehavior, will not only delay real and lasting improvement, but it can cause behavior to worsen.

Most difficult students have a history of misbehavior reaching as far back as preschool. Add the near-constant flow of pep-talks over the years, and you have a group of students who have heard it all.
When difficult students see how desperate you are for them to improve, you hand over much of the leverage you need to help them change their ways.

Eye contact and a nod from across the room, a knowing smile and a fist bump, a note folded over and waiting on their desk . . . these authentic moments between you mean the world to students labeled as “difficult.
x: Visible teacher desperation for a student's improvement hands that student leverage they can exploit to disrupt the classroom.
Linsin argues against the common practice of pulling difficult students aside for encouraging pep-talks, contending it can worsen behavior rather than improve it.
Most difficult students have heard so many pep-talks over the years that they've become jaded and adept at tuning them out or telling teachers what they want to hear.
Frequent pep-talks with difficult students can worsen behavior rather than improve it, contrary to common intuition.
Recommended alternatives are small, restrained, and private acknowledgments—eye contact, a nod, a fist bump—reserved for genuine, self-driven improvement.

t: Why You Should Never, Ever Confuse Accountability And Motivation ntability-and-motivation/
q: One reason many teachers struggle with classroom management is because they confuse motivation and accountability.
There are only two effective ways to hold students accountable. The first, which is a response to individual misbehavior, is to dispassionately follow your classroom management plan.
Both ways are action-oriented. In other words, you do something in response to misbehavior, which is a key characteristic of effective accountability.
Sometimes this tact is used in place of accountability and sometimes it’s used in addition to accountability—as in escorting a student to time-out while giving a lecture.
True accountability, on the other hand, as defined above, protects the student-teacher relationship. It’s never personal or hurtful.
Motivation, in an effective classroom management sense, is never negative and comes more from the classroom environment you keep than the words you use.
And it never, ever replaces, hinders, or weakens true accountability.
x: Linsin argues that many teachers struggle with classroom management because they conflate two separate processes.

He defines true accountability as strictly action-oriented—following a classroom management plan to enforce a consequence, or stopping and restarting a botched class-wide routine—with talk held to a minimum.
Effective accountability is action-oriented with minimal talk.
Mixing accountability and motivation (e.g., lecturing while walking a student to time-out) damages trust and increases misbehavior.

t: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 7 — Teach Character
q: But here's the bold claim I'll spend this post backing up: if you aim at the Common Core goals only by doing increased text complexity, close reading, arguing, mandatory talking, and writing like crazy, you or a large amount of your students will begin to hate your/their life.

It's about reality. And the reality is that if the goals laid out in the Common Core are to be met while retaining joy in our classrooms, we had better figure out how to teach our students not just how to deal with a complex text cognitively, but also how to develop the chops for dealing with difficulty, period.

Non-cognitive skills are those things that have nothing to do with IQ but are, in fact, pretty darn good at predicting whether or not you'll be successful. By calling them skills, we're saying that, just like dribbling a soccer ball or writing your name, they can be intentionally taught and intentionally practiced and intentionally mastered.

When I give a complex text to the whole class, my below-level readers need to know that what I'm expecting is a gritty reading of the text. They may not pull out as much as their at- or above-level peers, but I expect them to focus for the duration of the reading and to finish it.

The biggest reason our kids are starting to latch onto grit and self-control is probably because they hear them mentioned hundreds of times per week between our four classes. It's become part of the fabric of our classrooms.

But if you don't have such a luxury, the key with impacting students and colleagues is to simply get started in your own room. I am NOT advocating that you completely disregard your school's curriculum and policies — seven years into my career, I've come to realize that such behavior is usually 1) ineffective, 2) alienating, and 3) foolishly prideful. (Trust a guy who's been there.)

But our students also need to know how to deal with difficulty — not only how to deal with a difficult text, but how to deal with difficulty itself. Grit and self-control aren't the only way to teach them this but, in my opinion, they are the easiest, most straightforward, least complicated way.
x: Stuart's provocative claim is that a rigor-only push toward the Common Core will make teachers or students hate their lives unless students are also taught how to handle difficulty.
Stuart's provocative claim is that a rigor-only push toward the Common Core will make teachers or students hate their lives unless students are also taught how to handle difficulty.

Drawing on Paul Tough's How Children Succeed and KIPP's character strengths, he frames grit and self-control as non-cognitive skills that are learnable habits rather than inborn traits, and that strongly predict success.
He ties each strength to literacy work: below-level readers are expected to read a complex text grittily, and debaters are expected to show self-control toward opposing views.
Explicit lessons are only the introduction; the real driver is hearing the strengths named hundreds of times a week through specific, descriptive praise and letting students feel the payoff.
Teachers without a like-minded team should start in their own classroom alongside the existing curriculum, since defying school policy is usually ineffective, alienating and prideful.

t: How To Save Yourself A Mountain Of Stress And Misbehavior and-misbehavior/
q: Small, seemingly insignificant behaviors in September will in almost every circumstance multiply into major disruptions down the road.
Well, one of the truisms of classroom management is that little things don’t stay little for long.
Inconsistency communicates to students that you don’t mean what you say and therefore can’t be trusted.
The second common approach that leads to growing and pervading misbehavior is when teachers are unclear about what they expect from students. This is the “I’ll know it when I see it” approach.
The lesson here is that you can’t effectively hold students accountable for that which hasn’t been clearly and thoroughly defined for them.

The solution to both faulty approaches is to take the time to thoroughly teach what you expect from your students, from A to Z and back again, based on the clarity of what you want each day to look like.
